Monocots. These are flowering plants with a single cotyledon, or seed leaf. They make up roughly thirty percent of all angiosperm diversity, and they include grasses, sedges, lilies, orchids, palms, and bananas. Collectively, monocots are some of the most economically important plants on Earth, because they include wheat, rice, corn, and sugar cane.

That single cotyledon affects how the seedling develops and how the roots and shoots are structured differently compared to other plants. When you look at their leaves, they typically have parallel venation, with veins running side-by-side, rather than the branching net pattern you find in dicots. Inside the stem, vascular bundles are scattered throughout the cross-section rather than arranged in a ring, and there's no clear boundary between cortex and pith.

Instead of the deep taproot that many plants use, monocots typically develop a fibrous root system with many thin roots coming from the base, though some monocot trees like palms are exceptions. Their flowers are organized in a characteristic way: parts typically come in multiples of three, so you might see three sepals, three petals, and six stamens, rather than the multiples of four or five that other plants often use.

Monocots include the grasses, the Poaceae family, which is the most economically vital plant family we know, and also the orchids, which are the most diverse angiosperm family by far. You also find lilies, irises, and palms in this group. Monocots and dicots together comprise nearly all flowering plants, so understanding how these two groups differ is essential to understanding flowering plant diversity.
